A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same clinical text augmentation framework. All pages, including figures, tables, equations, and appendices, are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original augmentation-quality measurements, downstream clinical prediction results, component comparisons, distillation experiments, and hyperparameter sweeps.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, alternative entity-extractor evaluations, clinician annotations, and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: The weak-expert extraction, constrained prompting, generalist rewriting, candidate filtering, and DPO distillation procedures are retained. The prompt adds semantic-level wording but retains verbatim-preservation instructions; this does not establish a procedural change.

E1.justification: Both versions use MIMIC-III for readmission, mortality, length-of-stay, phenotyping, and ICD coding. The additional clinician annotations and model variants evaluate retained clinical-note coverage rather than introducing a new dataset, task, or input environment.

E2.justification: Beyond Naive and CATO, v2 evaluates BioMistral-7B, labeled Biomedical LLM, and SynName+SciName in the downstream and augmentation-quality comparisons (Tables 1–2). Table 12 also introduces an SFT comparator for the cost analysis, substantially broadening the alternatives evaluated.

E3.justification: V1 measures entity preservation and hallucination using the guidance extractor. V2 adds alternative NER evaluators, UMLS concept-level scoring, a three-clinician evaluation of 26 notes, and a controlled runtime comparison normalized to 300 notes. These substantially extend evaluation design without establishing that retained downstream experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds Medical-NER and BioMed-NER expert variants, evaluator-sensitivity comparisons (Tables 3 and 5), clinician-based validation and an omission case study (Appendix A.4, Figure 6), and cost analysis (Appendix A.5). The earlier generalist-size comparisons and hyperparameter sweeps remain.

E5.justification: Five-run means and standard errors and the statement about fixed seeds are retained. Appendix A.4 newly reports inter-annotator reliability using Fleiss’ Kappa for three clinicians: 0.437, 0.710, and 0.655 for readmission, mortality, and length-of-stay, respectively.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial baseline, concept-level, evaluator-robustness, clinician, and runtime results. For example, Table 11 reports proposed-method token PR/HR of 0.74/0.22 and concept PR/HR of 0.79/0.20; Table 12 reports 40.21 minutes versus 34.01 for Naive. Matching earlier downstream, ICD, distillation, and hyperparameter scores are retained.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 adds definitions of expert recall r and constraint-violation probability ε, and a conditional corruption bound rε + (1-r)p_c, with improvement claimed when ε < p_c and r > 0. This is a limited analytical addition; the existing augmentation and PR/HR equations remain substantively unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract broadens claimed superiority from existing LLM augmentation methods to both LLM-based and traditional augmentation, and explicitly claims token- and concept-level safety improvements. The central collaboration and expert-guidance distillation contributions remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretation through arguments about noisy-expert safety, evaluator independence, and efficiency relative to training-based augmentation. Appendix A.4 also identifies missed contextual or implicit clinical information as a concrete failure mode, extending v1’s more general discussion of detection calibration and domain expertise.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 explicitly states selected settings of learning rate 4×10^-5, LoRA rank 16, and three epochs, where v1 provided sweeps and recommendations. Appendix A.5 adds the V100 hardware, backbone, timing scope, and normalization details. These are documentation additions, not evidence of changed retained experiments.

R1.justification: V2 adds focused references including Abdollahi et al. on medical substitution, Labrak et al. on BioMistral, and Xu et al. on knowledge-infused clinical generation, alongside additional background and cost citations. Positioning expands to these alternatives while retaining the existing related-work framework.

P1.justification: V2 revises the abstract, reframes the problem as structure-aware augmentation, tightens experimental discussion, gives distillation its own subsection, and reorganizes the appendices. Author, affiliation, funding, and disclosure text also changes, but the main section sequence and substantial portions of the prose remain.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, with extensive rearrangement of displays. Existing explanatory figures and the ICD table move to the appendix, comparison tables expand, and new safety, evaluator, clinician, and cost tables plus a highlighted clinical case figure are added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central safety evidence by reducing dependence on v1’s potentially circular single-extractor evaluation through alternative NER evaluators, concept-level scoring, and clinician annotations. Broader baselines and an explicit failure case further improve credibility. The small clinician sample and incompletely specified SFT cost comparison remain limitations, but the independent validation addresses an important weakness in v1.
